claims.claim: The Altar Stone at the heart of Stonehenge came from northeast Scotland.
claims.note: Abstract: 'remarkable similarity to the Old Red Sandstone of the Orcadian Basin in northeast Scotland'; Discussion: data 'indicate that the Altar Stone of Stonehenge has a provenance from the ORS in the Orcadian Basin of northeast Scotland'. 'At the heart' matches 'The central megalith of Stonehenge, the Altar Stone (Stone 80)'. Region-level wording (no outcrop named) matches the paper.

claims.claim: (A4 hook) A viewer who swipes at second two leaves believing the Altar Stone, Stonehenge's central stone, originated in northeast Scotland.
claims.note: That takeaway is the paper's central finding as stated; no later sentence in the script is needed to make it true. The popular-myth risk (an actual altar) is not asserted: 'Altar Stone' is the stone's conventional name (Stone 80).

claims.claim: It is a six-tonne slab of sandstone, nearly five metres long.
claims.note: 'measuring 4.9 x 1.0 x 0.5 m ... weighing 6 t and composed of pale green micaceous sandstone'; abstract 'a 6 tonne shaped block', 'central recumbent sandstone megalith'. 4.9 m = 'nearly five metres'; 4.9 x 1.0 x 0.5 m fits 'slab'.

claims.claim: Several of Stonehenge's bluestones came from hills in west Wales, about two hundred and twenty-five kilometres away.
claims.note: 'the igneous bluestones were brought around 225 km from the Mynydd Preseli to Stonehenge' (citing Parker Pearson et al. 2020); Mynydd Preseli placed 'close to' Mill Bay, Pembrokeshire. 'Several' understates rather than overstates. 'Came from' is about origin only, so the glacial-transport minority view the paper mentions does not contradict it.

claims.claim: For about a hundred years, the Altar Stone was thought to come from Wales too.
claims.source_checked: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07652-1; Thomas 1923 doi:10.1017/S0003581500005096 (Cambridge Core landing page only, full text paywalled, metadata confirms author/title/July 1923)
claims.note: Clarke: early Mill Bay, Pembrokeshire source proposed in Thomas (1923); after Mill Bay was ruled out 'a source from elsewhere in the ORS of the Anglo-Welsh Basin was still considered likely', until Bevins et al. 2023 showed 'the Anglo-Welsh Basin is highly unlikely to be the source'. 1923 to 2023/2024 is about a century. Rests on Clarke's peer-reviewed account; Thomas's own text was not readable here.

claims.claim: Then geologists dated tiny mineral grains inside it.
claims.note: 'we present in situ U-Pb, Lu-Hf and trace element isotopic data for zircon, apatite and rutile from two fragments of the Altar Stone'; Methods: heavy-mineral grains 'typically 10-40 um wide'. The SOURCES quote is verified. Minor: zircon from the stone had already been dated in 2020 (Bevins et al., ref 1), but that does not make 'Then' false, because the 2024 dating is the one that produced the Scottish match.

claims.claim: Their ages matched old sandstone in northeast Scotland, at least seven hundred and fifty kilometres away.
claims.note: Abstract: 'remarkable similarity to the Old Red Sandstone of the Orcadian Basin in northeast Scotland. Such a provenance implies that the Altar Stone ... was sourced at least 750 km from its current location.' Apatite ages from Caithness and Orkney samples 'match those from the Altar Stone'. 'Old sandstone' is a loose rendering of 'Old Red Sandstone' (mostly Mid-Devonian per the paper) but is not false.

claims.claim: How six tonnes made that trip is unknown.
claims.note: The paper only infers the route ('suggests', 'we posit') from how hard overland transport would have been, with no direct evidence of the route or method. So 'unknown' is accurate.

claims.claim: The researchers think it probably went by sea.
claims.note: Abstract: 'The difficulty of long-distance overland transport of such massive cargo from Scotland, navigating topographic barriers, suggests that it was transported by sea.' Discussion says sea routes south from the Orcadian Basin were possible. 'Probably' matches 'suggests'.
